content: 1. Co-administration of piperacillin with immune checkpoint inhibitors may interfere with their therapeutic effects. Close monitoring is recommended. 2. Piperacillin can decrease the levels or effects of bazedoxifene/conjugated estrogens by altering intestinal flora. This interaction applies only to oral forms of the hormone. The risk of contraceptive failure is low, but caution and monitoring are advised. 3. Piperacillin reduces the effects of the BCG vaccine (live) through pharmacodynamic antagonism. This combination is contraindicated. Live bacterial vaccines should only be administered after completing antibiotic treatment, as antibiotics may diminish the therapeutic effects of BCG. 4. Piperacillin increases the levels or effects of bivalirudin through anticoagulation. Avoid this combination or use an alternative drug. 5. Cephalosporins may decrease prothrombin activity. Close monitoring is necessary. 6. Piperacillin reduces the effects of camrelizumab through an unspecified interaction mechanism. Caution and monitoring are advised. 7. Piperacillin reduces the effects of cemiplimab through an unspecified interaction mechanism. Caution and monitoring are advised. 8. Chloramphenicol decreases the effects of piperacillin through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Caution and monitoring are advised, as bacteriostatic agents may inhibit the effects of bactericidal agents. 9. Chlorothiazide increases piperacillin levels by decreasing renal clearance. This interaction is minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 10. Piperacillin reduces the effects of the cholera vaccine through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Avoid co-administration of the cholera vaccine with systemic antibiotics, as these agents may act against the vaccine strain. Do not administer the cholera vaccine to patients who have received oral or parenteral antibiotics within 14 days prior to vaccination. 11. Piperacillin increases the levels or effects of choline magnesium trisalicylate through acidic (anionic) drug competition for renal tubular clearance. This interaction is minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 12. Clarithromycin decreases the effects of piperacillin through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Caution and monitoring are advised, as bacteriostatic agents may inhibit the effects of bactericidal agents. 13. Piperacillin reduces the effects of cosibelimab through an unspecified interaction mechanism. Caution and monitoring are advised. 14. Piperacillin increases the effects of dalteparin through anticoagulation. Avoid this combination or use an alternative drug. Piperacillin can also inhibit platelet aggregation, so close monitoring is necessary. 15. Demeclocycline decreases the effects of piperacillin through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Caution and monitoring are advised, as bacteriostatic agents may inhibit the effects of bactericidal agents. 16. Dichlorphenamide and piperacillin both decrease serum potassium levels. Caution and monitoring are advised. 17. Piperacillin reduces the effects of dostarlimab through an unspecified interaction mechanism. Caution and monitoring are advised. 18. Doxycycline decreases the effects of piperacillin through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Caution and monitoring are advised, as bacteriostatic agents may inhibit the effects of bactericidal agents. 19. Piperacillin reduces the effects of durvalumab through an unspecified interaction mechanism. Caution and monitoring are advised. 20. Piperacillin increases the effects of enoxaparin through anticoagulation. Avoid this combination or use an alternative drug. Piperacillin can also inhibit platelet aggregation, so close monitoring is necessary. 21. Erythromycin base decreases the effects of piperacillin through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Caution and monitoring are advised, as bacteriostatic agents may inhibit the effects of bactericidal agents. 22. Caution and monitoring are advised, as bacteriostatic agents may inhibit the effects of bactericidal agents. 25. Piperacillin increases the effects of gentamicin through pharmacodynamic synergism. This interaction is minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 26. Piperacillin increases the levels or effects of heparin through anticoagulation. Avoid this combination or use an alternative drug. Piperacillin can also inhibit platelet aggregation. 27. Hydrochlorothiazide increases piperacillin levels by decreasing renal clearance. This interaction is minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 28. Piperacillin increases the levels or effects of ibuprofen IV through acidic (anionic) drug competition for renal tubular clearance. This interaction is minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 29. Piperacillin increases the levels or effects of meclofenamate through acidic (anionic) drug competition for renal tubular clearance. This interaction is minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 30. Piperacillin reduces the effects of microbiota oral formulations through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Avoid this combination or use an alternative drug. Antibacterial agents may decrease the efficacy of microbiota oral formulations containing bacterial spores. Complete antibiotic regimens 2–4 days before initiating microbiota oral therapy. 31. Minocycline decreases the effects of piperacillin through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Caution and monitoring are advised, as bacteriostatic agents may inhibit the effects of bactericidal agents. 32. Piperacillin increases the effects of neomycin PO through pharmacodynamic synergism. This interaction is minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 33. Piperacillin reduces the effects of nivolumab through an unspecified interaction mechanism. Caution and monitoring are advised. 34. Omadacycline decreases the effects of piperacillin through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Avoid this combination or use an alternative drug. Tetracyclines may interfere with the bactericidal action of penicillins. Monitor for decreased therapeutic effects of penicillins if used concomitantly with a tetracycline. 35. Piperacillin reduces the effects of penpulimab through an unspecified interaction mechanism. Caution and monitoring are advised. 37. Rose hips increase the levels or effects of piperacillin through acidic (anionic) drug competition for renal tubular clearance. This interaction is minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 40. Sarecycline decreases the effects of piperacillin through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Avoid this combination or use an alternative drug. Tetracyclines may interfere with the bactericidal action of penicillins. Monitor for decreased therapeutic effects of penicillins if used concomitantly with a tetracycline. 41. Piperacillin reduces the effects of sintilimab through an unspecified interaction mechanism. Caution and monitoring are advised. 42. Piperacillin reduces the effects of sodium picosulfate/magnesium oxide/anhydrous citric acid by altering metabolism. Caution and monitoring are advised, as antibiotics may decrease efficacy by altering colonic bacterial flora needed to convert sodium picosulfate to its active form. 43. Piperacillin increases the effects of streptomycin through pharmacodynamic synergism. This interaction is minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 44. Tetracycline decreases the effects of piperacillin through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Caution and monitoring are advised, as bacteriostatic agents may inhibit the effects of bactericidal agents. 45. Piperacillin reduces the effects of tislelizumab through an unspecified interaction mechanism. Caution and monitoring are advised. 46. Piperacillin increases the effects of tobramycin through pharmacodynamic synergism. This interaction is minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 47. Piperacillin reduces the effects of toripalimab through an unspecified interaction mechanism. Caution and monitoring are advised. 48. Piperacillin increases the toxicity of vancomycin through an unspecified interaction mechanism. Caution and monitoring are advised. Monitor kidney function in patients receiving both piperacillin and vancomycin. 49. Piperacillin increases the toxicity of vecuronium through pharmacodynamic synergism. Modify therapy and monitor closely, as neuromuscular blockade may be prolonged. 50. Piperacillin and warfarin may increase each other's effects through pharmacodynamic synergism. Modify therapy and monitor closely. Platelet dysfunction can occur with extended-spectrum penicillins. Monitor INR and adjust warfarin dose if needed. 51. Piperacillin increases the levels or effects of willow bark through acidic (anionic) drug competition for renal tubular clearance. This interaction is minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 52. Serious adverse effects of piperacillin include anaphylaxis, agranulocytosis, thrombocytopenia, eosinophilia, melena, leukopenia, positive Coombs test, prolonged PT and PTT, transient LFT and creatinine elevations, seizures, pulmonary edema, pulmonary embolism, hepatitis, jaundice, hemolytic anemia, pancytopenia, hypersensitivity reactions, interstitial nephritis, and severe skin reactions (e.g., Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis). 53. Monitor renal, hepatic, and hematopoietic functions during prolonged treatment. Prolonged use may result in fungal or bacterial superinfections. 54. Administering piperacillin without a proven or strongly suspected bacterial infection or prophylactic indication increases the risk of drug-resistant bacteria. 55. Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD) has been reported. If CDAD is suspected or confirmed, discontinue ongoing antibacterial drug use not directed against C. difficile and implement appropriate management. 56. Piperacillin contains sodium, which may require caution in patients with sodium restrictions. Periodic electrolyte monitoring is recommended, especially in patients with low potassium reserves or those receiving cytotoxic therapy or diuretics. 57. Increased frequency of fever and rash has been reported in cystic fibrosis patients receiving piperacillin. 58. Use caution in patients with renal impairment or underdeveloped kidneys due to sodium load and potential adverse effects of high serum penicillin concentrations. Dose adjustment may be necessary. 59. High doses of piperacillin administered intravenously, particularly in the presence of renal failure, may cause neuromuscular excitability or seizures. Monitor patients with renal impairment or seizure disorders closely for signs of neuromuscular excitability or seizures. 60. Cases of hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) have been reported in pediatric and adult patients. Signs and symptoms of HLH include fever, rash, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and cytopenia. If HLH is suspected, discontinue therapy immediately and initiate appropriate management. 61. Piperacillin and tazobactam cross the placenta in humans. Insufficient data are available to determine the risk of major birth defects or miscarriage. 62. Piperacillin is excreted in human milk, but tazobactam concentrations in human milk have not been studied. The effects on breastfed children or milk production are unknown. 63. Prolonged therapy (≥21 days) with piperacillin may be associated with leukopenia or neutropenia. Periodic assessment of hematopoietic function is recommended. 64. Serious skin reactions, including Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, have been reported. Discontinue therapy if such reactions occur. 65. Cases of hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) have been reported. If HLH is suspected, discontinue therapy immediately and initiate appropriate management.
